title: Hourly Employee Labor Laws: 2026 Guide for Small Businesses
summary: Learn what hourly employee labor laws require in 2026, from overtime and exempt status to tip credits and breaks, plus how state rules change the picture.
body_markdown:
In 2023, a[federal jury awarded $22.25 million](https://www.dol.gov/newsroom/releases/whd/whd20230510) to employees at a manufacturer who weren’t paid for the time they spent changing into protective gear and showering at work. The Third Circuit[upheld the award](https://www.supremecourt.gov/DocketPDF/24/24A990/355546/20250414163124983_FINAL%20Appendix%20-%20350875496-v1.pdf) in December 2024.


That’s an extreme case. Most violations are much smaller: a few unpaid minutes at the time clock, overtime figured on the wrong rate, or a manager who was never exempt to begin with.


Bryan Tublin, co-founder and CEO of[Kitava](https://www.joinhomebase.com/customers/kitava-kitchen-case-study-schedule) , a multi-location food and beverage business, remembers when time tracking was “a very trust-based system” with no “good guardrails around being able to verify accuracy.” Here’s what hourly employee labor laws require in 2026, so you can check your own practices against them.


## **Hourly Employee Labor Laws in 2026**


Federal law sets the baseline for hourly employee labor laws, states can add stricter rules, and you follow whichever is stricter. The main points for 2026:


- **Minimum wage:** $7.25 an hour federally, with many states higher
- **Overtime:** 1.5 times the regular rate for hours over 40 in a workweek, for non-exempt employees under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA)
- **Exempt status:** A salary basis, at least $684 a week, and a duties test. Hourly pay generally means non-exempt.
- **Hours worked:** Pay for all time worked, including some tasks before and after a shift
- **Tipped employees:** A $2.13 cash wage with up to a $5.12 tip credit
- **Records:** Keep payroll records three years and time cards two


The table below shows the full 2026 federal picture.

## **2026 Federal Wage and Hour Laws at a Glance for Hourly Employees**


Federal wage and hour laws, set mostly by the FLSA, cover the minimum wage, overtime, recordkeeping, and child labor limits for most US employers. These figures are the federal floor for 2026, and your state may require more.


2026 Federal Wage and Hour Laws at a Glance for Hourly Employees Rule 2026 federal requirement


[Minimum wage](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/minimum-wage) $7.25 an hour


[Tipped cash wage and tip credit](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/fact-sheets/15-tipped-employees-flsa) $2.13 an hour cash wage, up to a $5.12 an hour tip credit


[Overtime](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/overtime) 1.5 times the regular rate over 40 hours in a workweek (non-exempt employees)


[Exempt salary minimum](https://www.dol.gov/newsroom/releases/whd/whd20260514) $684 a week (or $35,568 a year), plus salary basis and duties tests


[Highly compensated employee](https://www.dol.gov/newsroom/releases/whd/whd20260514) $107,432 a year, including at least $684 a week on a salary or fee basis


[Payroll records](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/flsa-recordkeeping-requirement-time-cards) Keep for three years


[Time cards and schedules](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/fact-sheets/21-flsa-recordkeeping) Keep for two years


[Statute of limitations](https://www.dol.gov/general/topic/wages/backpay) Two years, or three years for willful violations


[Civil penalty](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/labor-law-consequences) Up to $2,515 per repeated or willful violation


Federal figures reviewed November 2026. States may set higher minimums, so check your state’s rules.


## **Who Does the Fair Labor Standards Act Cover?**


FLSA stands for the[Fair Labor Standards Act](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/flsa) , the federal law behind minimum wage, overtime, recordkeeping, and child labor standards. It applies through enterprise coverage and individual coverage, and together they reach most hourly employees.


- **Enterprise coverage:**[Applies to](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/fact-sheets/14-flsa-coverage) businesses with at least two employees and $500,000 or more in annual sales, plus hospitals, schools, and government agencies of any size
- **Individual coverage:** Applies to employees whose work involves interstate commerce, which courts read broadly enough to cover most hourly workers


State and local laws can add protections on top, and the FLSA limits the hours and jobs minors can work. Which federal laws apply to you can also shift with[business size](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/labor-laws-employee-count) .


## **Is an Hourly Employee Exempt Under Federal Labor Laws?**


Most hourly employees are non-exempt, so they’re owed overtime. An employee is exempt only if they’re paid on a salary basis, earn at least $684 a week (or $35,568 a year), and meet a duties test. Hourly pay generally rules out exempt status, and a job title never creates it.


1. **Salary basis:** A set salary that generally doesn’t change with the quality or amount of work
2. **Salary level:** At least[$684 a week](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/federal-overtime-salary-threshold) . After courts vacated a 2024 increase, the Department of Labor (DOL)[restored the 2019 level in May 2026](https://www.dol.gov/newsroom/releases/whd/whd20260514) .
3. **Duties:** Day-to-day work that fits an executive, administrative, professional, computer, or outside sales exemption


Highly compensated employees need $107,432 in total annual compensation, including at least $684 a week, and face a lighter duties test. Some states, including California and New York, set higher exempt salary minimums, so check yours before you reclassify anyone.


A flat salary won’t protect you. The DOL found that a Florida restaurant paid most employees monthly salaries of $1,000 to $3,000 even though they typically worked more than 40 hours a week, and it[recovered $732,976 for 31 workers](https://www.dol.gov/newsroom/releases/whd/whd20260903) . At $1,000 a month and 40 hours a week, that’s about $5.77 an hour, below the federal minimum wage.

### **Common Exempt Classification Mistakes**


- **Trusting a manager title:** A title alone never makes someone exempt
- **Overlooking duties:** An employee paid above $684 a week who spends most of the day on non-exempt work, like a shift lead working the floor, may still be owed overtime
- **Docking pay for partial-day absences:** This can jeopardize the salary basis
- **Paying a flat monthly salary without checking duties:** This is common in restaurants and retail, and it’s the pattern behind the case above


If an employee sues, you can owe back pay plus an equal amount in liquidated damages, unless you can show you acted in good faith. Getting[classification right](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/overtime-exempt-employees-classification-costs) comes down to what people do all day, not what you call them.


## **Hourly Employee Labor Laws on Pay: Minimum Wage, Tips, and Hours Worked**


Four pay rules trip up hourly teams most often.


### **Federal Minimum Wage and How State Minimums Interact**


The federal minimum wage is $7.25 an hour, and it hasn’t changed since July 2009. Most employees earn more, because many states and cities set higher rates. When the two differ, you pay whichever is higher.


In 2026,[California’s minimum wage is $16.90](https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/faq_minimumwage.htm) ,[Washington’s is $17.13](https://lni.wa.gov/workers-rights/wages/minimum-wage/) , and[New York’s ranges from $16.00 to $17.00](https://dol.ny.gov/minimum-wage) depending on location. Tip credits, piece-rate pay, and bonuses can also change what you owe, so check each calculation before payroll runs.


### **What Is a Tip Credit and Is $2.13 an Hour Legal?**


A tip credit lets you count part of an employee’s tips toward the minimum wage. Under federal law, you can pay a tipped employee a $2.13 cash wage if tips bring them to at least $7.25 an hour, a credit of up to $5.12. The employee must customarily earn more than $30 a month in tips, and you must make up any shortfall.


Before you take the credit, tell employees the cash wage, the credit amount, and that they keep their tips except in a valid tip pool. You can’t keep any employee tips, and managers and supervisors can’t take from a tip pool. Some states, including California, Washington, and Minnesota, ban the tip credit entirely.


### **What Counts as Compensable Time**


The FLSA’s definition of compensable time is broader than most employers expect. You have to pay employees for:


- **Pre-shift and post-shift tasks** that are integral to the job, like a butcher sharpening knives before a shift
- **On-call time** when employees can’t use the time for their own purposes
- **Required training** that relates to the job
- **Travel between job sites** during the workday, though regular commuting generally doesn’t count


The test is whether the activity is[primarily for your benefit](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/fact-sheets/22-flsa-hours-worked) . If it is, it likely counts as work.


### **The 7-Minute Rule for Clocking In**


The 7-minute rule lets you round clock-in and clock-out times to the nearest quarter hour. If an employee clocks in at 8:07am, you can round back to 8:00. At 8:08am, it rounds forward to 8:15.


The FLSA[allows rounding](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-V/subchapter-B/part-785/subpart-D/section-785.48) to the nearest five minutes, tenth of an hour, or quarter hour, but only if it averages out so employees get paid for all the time they work. A practice that consistently favors you is the problem.


## **Federal Overtime Laws for Hourly Employees**


### **When Overtime Pay Is Required Under the FLSA**


Non-exempt employees must be paid[at least 1.5 times](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/overtime) their regular rate for every hour over 40 in a workweek. A workweek is any fixed, recurring period of 168 hours, or seven consecutive 24-hour periods. It doesn’t have to match the calendar week.


Overtime is counted per workweek, not per pay period. So if you pay biweekly, you still calculate each seven-day week separately.


Amy Marella, who owns a retail shop called The Hidden Garden, has seen how fast it adds up. “We’ll get last-minute orders or something will happen,” she says. “Someone needs something, and it causes everyone to go into two hours of overtime or three hours of overtime.”


### **How to Calculate FLSA Overtime**


Overtime is based on the regular rate, and that includes more than the hourly wage. Nondiscretionary bonuses, commissions, and shift differentials count too. Divide total pay for the week by total hours worked, then pay half that rate again for each overtime hour. Here’s an example for an employee who earns $20 an hour, works 45 hours, and earns a $90 production bonus:


1. **Straight-time pay:** 45 hours × $20 = $900
2. **Add the bonus:** $900 + $90 = $990
3. **Regular rate:** $990 ÷ 45 hours = $22
4. **Overtime premium:** 5 hours × $11 (half of $22) = $55
5. **Total pay:** $990 + $55 = $1,045


Figuring overtime on the $20 base rate alone would pay $1,040, which leaves the employee $5 short. Repeated across a team, week after week, gaps like that turn into back wages.


Cambria Wallace, a payroll operations project lead at Homebase, suggests lining up your workweek with your pay period. Make sure “the start day of your ‘Workweek’ matches up with the start day of your pay period,” she says, which “makes for less confusing payouts to employees.”


Homebase sends[overtime alerts](https://www.joinhomebase.com/time-clock/overtime) when an employee approaches or reaches overtime, so you can adjust the schedule before payday.


### **Can an Employee Be Forced to Work Overtime?**


In most states, yes. Federal law doesn’t bar[mandatory overtime](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/is-mandatory-overtime-legal) for adult workers, and employees who refuse can face discipline. Some states and industries, such as nursing, limit it.


### **How Many Hours Can an Hourly Employee Legally Work?**


For most adults, no federal law caps the hours in a day or week. The FLSA only requires overtime pay once weekly hours pass 40.[Commercial truck drivers](https://www.fmcsa.dot.gov/regulations/hours-service/summary-hours-service-regulations) and[airline flight crews](https://www.faa.gov/faq/what-are-crewmember-flight-and-duty-time-and-rest-requirements) are the main exceptions, with federal limits set for safety. Minors face hour limits under the FLSA, and some states add daily overtime, covered below.


## **Federal Labor Laws on Breaks for Hourly Employees**


### **What Federal Law Says About Meal and Rest Breaks**


Federal law doesn’t require meal or rest breaks for adult workers. It does set rules for the breaks you offer:


- **Short breaks:** Rest breaks of about five to 20 minutes must be paid
- **Meal breaks:** Periods of 30 minutes or more can be unpaid only if the employee is completely relieved of duty


Automatic meal deductions only work if employees are fully relieved. A break spent answering questions or watching the floor counts as work time.


Kitava wanted a way to back up its practices. Bryan Tublin says it needed to confirm “that they are taking their breaks and they’re clocking in and out for their breaks legally and appropriately.”


### **State Break Laws Where the Rules Are Stricter**


[California](https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/faq_restperiods.htm) requires a paid 10-minute rest break for every four hours worked.[New York](https://dol.ny.gov/day-rest-and-meal-periods) requires an unpaid 30-minute meal break for shifts over six hours. Oregon, Washington, and Colorado have detailed rules too.


Where state law asks for more, state law wins. Homebase lets you set[break rules and reminders](https://www.joinhomebase.com/time-clock/break-management) for your team.


## **State Labor Laws for Hourly Employees**


Federal law is the floor. States can set higher minimums, daily overtime, stricter breaks, and extra pay rules. These two sit at opposite ends.


### **New York Hourly Employee Labor Laws**


[New York’s labor laws](https://www.joinhomebase.com/state-labor-laws/new-york) are among the most employee-protective in the country:


- **Minimum wage:** $17.00 an hour in New York City, Long Island, and Westchester County, and $16.00 elsewhere as of 2026
- **Spread of hours:** Employees whose workday spans more than 10 hours may be owed an extra hour of pay
- **Call-in pay:** Employees sent home early may be owed at least four hours of pay, or three for hotel and restaurant workers
- **Meal breaks:** A 30-minute unpaid break for shifts over six hours


### **Texas Labor Laws for Hourly Employees**


Texas largely follows federal law, which gives employers more flexibility. The minimum wage is the federal $7.25, overtime follows the FLSA with no daily threshold, and adults have no required breaks. Texas is also an at-will state.


### **States With Daily Overtime Laws**


Federal overtime is weekly, but a few states count daily hours too.[California](https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/faq_overtime.htm) requires overtime after eight hours in a day and double time after 12. Alaska requires it after eight hours in a day, Colorado after 12 hours in a day or 12 consecutive hours, and Nevada after eight for employees earning under 1.5 times the state minimum wage.


### **How to Find Your State’s Employment Standards**


Employment standards change often, so go to your state’s Department of Labor for the latest rules. Homebase also keeps[state labor laws](https://www.joinhomebase.com/state-labor-laws) guides covering minimum wage, overtime, and breaks, so you can check yours in one place.


## **Common Hourly Employee Labor Law Mistakes and How to Avoid Them**


### **Misclassifying Employees vs. Independent Contractors**


Misclassifying an employee as an independent contractor is one of the costliest wage and hour mistakes. Contractors aren’t covered by minimum wage or overtime rules, so a mistake can mean back wages, unpaid overtime, and penalties.


The DOL and courts use multi-factor tests, and the bar for true contractor status is higher than many employers assume. Start with the[DOL’s worker classification guidance](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/flsa/misclassification) , and bring in an employment attorney for close calls.


### **Off-the-Clock Work and Employer Liability**


If you know, or should know, that someone is working off the clock,[that time is compensable](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/flsa/off-the-clock) . The usual culprits are unpaid pre-shift meetings, after-hours messages, and closing tasks after clock-out. A written policy against off-the-clock work, paired with a time clock that captures every hour, closes most of the gap.


### **Recordkeeping Requirements Under the FLSA**


The FLSA requires records for each employee, including name, address, occupation, hours worked each day and week, and wages paid each pay period. The retention periods are in the table above. Good records are also your best defense in a dispute.


Bryan Tublin at Kitava says employees and managers can now add notes to a time card when something needs to change. “If we do have to make a change, we can say, ‘Hey, you know, they told their manager they forgot to clock out for their break, so that’s why this adjustment is being made.’ And there’s a record of all that.”


## **How to Stay Compliant With Hourly Employee Labor Laws**


### **How to Keep Up With Labor Law Changes**


Labor laws change more often than most owners expect. Minimum wages rise, scheduling laws pass, and[federal rules shift](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/federal-labor-law-changes) too, as the exempt salary threshold did in 2026. Check your state’s Department of Labor at least once a year, subscribe to updates from the[DOL’s Wage and Hour Division](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd) , and review your employee handbook annually.


### **How Time Tracking Supports Labor Law Compliance**


Accurate time tracking is the base for everything above. When hours are captured automatically, overtime math is more reliable, off-the-clock work is harder to miss, and records are easier to keep. Cambria Wallace’s advice is simple: “Keep up with timecards daily so you are not surprised by the numbers of hours worked and OT amounts on payroll day.”

Call an employment attorney if you’re facing a wage claim, unsure how to classify a worker, expanding into a new state, or changing your pay structure. A short consultation usually costs far less than a back-wage claim.


## **Frequently Asked Questions About Hourly Employee Labor Laws**


### **What Is the 7 Minute Rule for Clocking In?**


The 7-minute rule lets employers round time clock punches to the nearest quarter hour. Punches in the first seven minutes of a quarter hour round down, and punches from minute eight onward round up. Rounding is legal only if it is neutral over time and does not consistently cut into what employees earn.


### **Is $2.13 an Hour Legal?**


Yes, in a narrow case. Federal law lets employers pay tipped employees a $2.13 cash wage if tips bring them to at least $7.25 an hour, a tip credit of up to $5.12. The employee must customarily earn more than $30 a month in tips, and the employer must cover any shortfall. Some states ban the tip credit.


### **Is an Hourly Employee Exempt or Nonexempt?**


Most hourly employees are non-exempt, which means they are owed overtime. An employee is exempt only if they are paid on a salary basis, earn at least $684 a week (or $35,568 a year), and meet a duties test. Hourly pay generally rules out exempt status, and a job title never creates it.


### **How Do You Calculate FLSA Overtime?**


Divide total weekly pay, including nondiscretionary bonuses and shift differentials, by total hours worked to get the regular rate. Then pay half that rate again for each hour over 40 in the workweek. Overtime is counted per workweek, not per pay period.


### **What States Have Daily Overtime Laws?**


California requires overtime after eight hours in a day and double time after 12. Alaska requires overtime after eight hours in a day, Colorado after 12 hours in a day or 12 consecutive hours, and Nevada after eight for employees earning under 1.5 times the state minimum wage. Federal law only counts weekly hours over 40.


### **What Is the FLSA Salary Threshold for 2026?**


The federal salary threshold is $684 a week (or $35,568 a year) for most white-collar exemptions. Highly compensated employees must earn at least $107,432 a year in total compensation, including at least $684 a week paid on a salary or fee basis. All exempt employees must also meet a duties test, and some states set higher thresholds.


### **Are Salaried Employees Always Exempt From Overtime?**


No. A salaried employee is exempt only if they earn at least $684 a week and also pass a duties test. Many salaried workers, such as a shift lead who spends the day on the floor or a restaurant worker on a flat monthly salary, are still owed overtime.
